questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix $A$ above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=10.$ Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{T}\,AP.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Note that $A$ is symmetric. Therefore, it is orthogonally diagonalizable. Let's now go through the process.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we already have the eigenvalues of $A:$

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=5\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=10$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 10\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Computing $A-(-2)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm, we obtain the second column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}]
$$

$$

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}],

where $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{13}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm, we obtain the second column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2\sqrt{13}}{13} \\ -\frac{3\sqrt{13}}{13}\end{aligned}]

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix $A$ above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{T}\,AP.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Note that $A$ is symmetric. Therefore, it is orthogonally diagonalizable. Let's now go through the process.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we already have the eigenvalues of $A:$

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-1$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]+1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}8 & -4 \\ -4 & -7\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix $A$ above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=9$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-8.$ Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{T}\,AP.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Note that $A$ is symmetric. Therefore, it is orthogonally diagonalizable. Let's now go through the process.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we already have the eigenvalues of $A:$

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=9\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-8$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=9,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-9I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -4 \\ -4 & -7\end{aligned}]-9[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -4 \\ -4 & -16\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-8I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{17},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-8)I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -4 \\ -4 & -7\end{aligned}]+8[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}16 & -4 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-8)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{17},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}}\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 \\ 0 & -8\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} & \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}}\end{aligned}]
$$
